analogy.p: A recipe lists ingredients (inputs), the cooking steps (processes) and the finished dish (output). It has to be in the right order and clear enough that anyone could follow it without guessing. Pseudocode is the written recipe, a flowchart is the same recipe drawn as a map with arrows, and real code is the recipe translated into the exact language of the kitchen robot that will cook it. A loop is like 'keep stirring until the sauce thickens' and a decision is like 'if the mixture is too dry, add water, otherwise carry on'. The analogy breaks down because a person can cope with a vague step such as 'add a pinch of salt', whereas a computer needs every instruction to be exact and unambiguous.
analogy.t: An algorithm is like a recipe, and a flowchart is the recipe drawn as a map

bullets: **Inputs** are the values the algorithm receives, for example a number typed in by the user, a value read from a file or a parameter passed to a subprogram.
**Processes** are the calculations and decisions carried out on the data, such as adding, comparing, looping or sorting.
**Outputs** are the results the algorithm produces, for example text printed on screen, a value returned from a function or data written to a file.
Algorithms use just three building blocks: **sequence** (steps one after another), **selection** (choosing a path with if/else) and **iteration** (repeating steps in a loop).
An algorithm is **not tied to a language**: the same algorithm can be written as a flowchart, as pseudocode or as real code in a language such as Python.

Exam tasks fall into four types: **interpret** (say what it does or what it outputs), **trace** (complete a trace table), **complete/correct** (fill gaps or fix errors) and **write** (create an algorithm from a description).
Always say **why** an algorithm is needed: a clear, correct plan lets a programmer write code that is right first time and lets other people understand and maintain it.
core.h: What an algorithm is and what the exam expects
core.p: An **algorithm** is a step-by-step set of instructions that solves a problem or completes a task. To be useful it must be **unambiguous** (each step can only be read one way), **finite** (it eventually stops) and **in the correct order**. OCR J277 asks you to design, create, interpret, correct, complete and refine algorithms, so you must be able to read an algorithm that is already written as well as write your own. Every algorithm can be broken into **inputs** (the data it needs), **processes** (what it does to that data) and **outputs** (what it gives back), and identifying these three parts is the first step in planning any solution.

bullets: Flowchart strengths: **visual**, shows the flow of control and branching clearly, good for explaining logic to non-programmers; weakness: takes space and becomes messy for large programs.
Pseudocode strengths: **quick to write**, compact, easy to convert into real code, no need to worry about exact syntax; weakness: no fixed standard unless a reference language is used.
Real code strengths: it can be **run and tested**; weakness: syntax must be exactly right, so it is slower to draft.
In the exam, **minor syntax slips are not penalised** if the intended logic is clear, but missing structure (no loop, wrong condition, no output) loses marks.
Use the style you are most accurate in; mixing styles in one answer is risky because the examiner may not be able to follow the logic.
Link to other topics: planning with flowcharts or pseudocode sits within the **program development** stages (analyse, design, code, test) and helps decomposition by showing each sub-task.
core.h: Three ways to present an algorithm: flowchart, pseudocode and code
core.p: A **flowchart** is a diagram that uses standard shapes joined by arrows to show the order of steps and decisions. **Pseudocode** is a structured, plain-language way of writing the steps that looks like code but does not have to obey the strict rules of any real language. OCR also publishes its own **OCR Reference Language**, a consistent pseudocode style used in the exam papers. A **high-level language** such as Python can also be used, and in the written paper you may answer in pseudocode, OCR Reference Language or your chosen programming language provided the logic is clear and correct. Each form suits a different audience: a flowchart is easy to see at a glance, pseudocode is quick to write and close to final code.

bullets: Every flowchart needs **one Start** and at least one **End** terminator.
Rectangle = process, **diamond = decision**, parallelogram = input or output, rounded rectangle = start/end, double-sided rectangle = subroutine call.
Label **both** exits from a decision (Yes/No or True/False); an unlabelled branch loses marks.
Write text inside shapes in the form of an instruction, for example total = total + 1 in a process or count < 5 ? in a decision.
Arrows must have **arrowheads** and should not cross unnecessarily; a loop is drawn by an arrow that returns to an earlier point.
Do not put a process or a calculation inside a decision diamond: the diamond only asks a question.
A common mistake is to use a rectangle for an input or output; use the **parallelogram**.
core.h: Flowchart symbols and the rules for drawing them
core.p: Flowcharts use a small set of agreed symbols and you must use the correct shape for each job. A **terminator** (rounded rectangle) marks the start and the end. A **process** (rectangle) shows an action such as a calculation or assignment. A **decision** (diamond) asks a question with exactly two outcomes, normally Yes and No, so each decision has one arrow in and two arrows out, each labelled. An **input/output** shape (parallelogram) is used when data is entered or displayed. A **subroutine** (rectangle with double vertical sides) calls a separate named subprogram. **Flow lines** with arrowheads show the direction in which the algorithm moves.

bullets: Trace a flowchart by writing the **current value of each variable** next to the step; do not try to hold it in your head.
A decision that sends an arrow **back upwards** creates a loop; the other exit leaves the loop.
Check the test carefully: n == 0 tests equality, while n = 0 in a process box would assign a value.
In the Even/Odd example, **n MOD 2 == 0** is true for even numbers because an even number leaves remainder 0 when divided by 2.
Both branches after the Even/Odd test return to the input step, so the program repeats until the user types 0.
Link to other topics: the structure of selection and iteration in a flowchart matches **if** and **while** in code, so converting between the two is a core skill.
When asked to **complete** a flowchart, check each missing shape type as well as its text: a missing diamond needs a question and two labelled arrows.
core.h: Reading and drawing flowcharts with decisions and loops
core.p: To follow a flowchart, start at the Start terminator and obey one arrow at a time, updating the values of the variables as you go. At a decision diamond test the condition using the current values and follow the matching branch. A **loop** appears in a flowchart whenever an arrow leads back to a point that has already been visited; the decision that controls the way out of the loop is the loop condition. When drawing your own, plan the inputs first, add the decision for each choice, and make sure every path eventually reaches an End so the algorithm cannot run forever by mistake. Fig 2 shows a loop that keeps reading numbers until 0 is entered.

bullets: Assignment: **variable = value**, read as 'the variable becomes this value', e.g. total = total + 5.
Constants: const VAT = 20 means VAT cannot be changed later; use them for fixed values such as tax rates or pi.
Input: age = input("Enter age") always gives the data as a **string** unless you cast it (see casting).
Output: print("Hello " + name) joins strings with **+**; this is called concatenation.
Comments: // this is a comment explains the code and is ignored when the program runs.
Use **meaningful names** such as totalCost instead of x; this makes algorithms easier to read and maintain.
Variable names cannot contain spaces and normally start with a letter; stick to simple names in the exam.
core.h: OCR Reference Language: variables, constants, input and output
core.p: A **variable** is a named location in memory whose value can change while the program runs, and a **constant** is a named value that cannot change once set. In OCR Reference Language you create or change a variable simply by assigning to it with a single equals sign, for example score = 0. Constants are declared with the keyword const. **Input** uses the input function with a prompt, and the result is assigned to a variable, for example name = input("Enter your name"). **Output** uses print, for example print(name). Text in speech marks is a string, and comments begin with two slashes so that humans can read notes the computer ignores.

bullets: **17 MOD 5 = 2** because 5 goes into 17 three times (15) leaving a remainder of 2.
**17 DIV 5 = 3** because 5 goes into 17 three whole times, ignoring the remainder.
**2 ^ 3 = 8** because 2 x 2 x 2 = 8; the ^ operator is exponentiation.
**x MOD 2 == 0** is a standard test for an **even** number and x MOD 2 == 1 for an odd positive number.
**AND**: age >= 13 AND age <= 19 is true only for ages 13 to 19 inclusive; **OR**: day == "Sat" OR day == "Sun" is true at weekends.
Use **NOT** to reverse a condition, e.g. NOT found is true while found is False.
Brackets control order of operations: (2 + 3) * 4 = 20 whereas 2 + 3 * 4 = 14 because multiplication is done first.
Common slip: writing x = 5 in a condition; the comparison needs ==.
core.p: Operators are symbols that act on values. **Arithmetic operators** are + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide), ^ (exponent, meaning to the power of), **MOD** (the remainder after division) and **DIV** (integer division, the whole number of times one number goes into another). **Comparison operators** produce True or False: == (equal to), != (not equal to), < (less than), <= (less than or equal to), > (greater than) and >= (greater than or equal to). **Boolean (logical) operators** combine conditions: AND is true only if both parts are true, OR is true if at least one part is true and NOT reverses the result. Be careful that a single = assigns a value whereas a double == compares.

bullets: Layout: if mark >= 70 then / print("Distinction") / elseif mark >= 50 then / print("Pass") / else / print("Fail") / endif.
Only **one branch** of an if/elseif/else block runs, so the **order** of conditions matters: test the most restrictive condition first.
Indent the code inside each branch to show the structure; examiners rely on this to read your logic.
switch is tidier than many elseif lines when comparing one variable with several fixed values, e.g. menu choices.
Switch layout: switch day: then case "Sat": print("Weekend") then default: print("Weekday") then endswitch.
Nested selection places one if inside another; every if needs its own **endif**.
Link to other topics: Boolean logic and truth tables (Paper 1) explain how AND/OR/NOT combine in conditions.
core.h: Selection: if, elseif, else and switch
core.p: **Selection** lets an algorithm choose between different paths depending on a condition. In OCR Reference Language the structure is: if condition then, followed by the instructions to run, optional elseif condition then branches, an optional else branch for everything left over, and it is closed with endif. The conditions are tested from top to bottom and only the first branch whose condition is true runs; the rest are skipped. A **switch** statement chooses between many fixed values of one variable using case labels, an optional default for anything unmatched, and finishes with endswitch. Selection is shown in a flowchart as a decision diamond.

bullets: **for i = 1 to 5** ... **next i** repeats 5 times (i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5); the counter changes automatically.
**while** loop: while answer != "yes" ... endwhile checks first and may never run if the condition is False at the start.
**do ... until** loop: the instructions run once before the condition until answer == "yes" is first checked.
Use **for** when you know how many repetitions you need and a condition-controlled loop when you do not, such as repeating until a correct password is entered.
An **infinite loop** happens if nothing inside the loop ever makes the condition change, e.g. forgetting count = count + 1.
**Off-by-one** errors are common: for i = 0 to 5 runs 6 times, not 5.
Loops can be **nested**: an inner loop runs completely for every pass of the outer loop, so a 3 by 4 nested loop runs the inner body 12 times.
Validation uses loops: keep asking while the input is not in the allowed range.
core.h: Iteration: for, while and do until loops
core.p: **Iteration** means repeating a block of instructions. A **count-controlled loop** repeats a set number of times and uses for: for i = 0 to 7 ... next i runs eight times because both the start value 0 and the end value 7 are included. A step can be added, for example for i = 2 to 10 step 2. A **condition-controlled loop** repeats until or while a condition holds. A while ... endwhile loop tests the condition **before** each pass, so it may run zero times. A do ... until condition loop tests **after** the body, so it always runs at least once. Using the wrong kind of loop or the wrong boundary is a very common source of marks being lost.

bullets: An array of size 5 has indexes **0, 1, 2, 3, 4**; using index 5 would cause an error because it does not exist.
Access: print(names[2]) outputs the **third** item because counting starts at 0.
Use a **for loop** to visit each element: for i = 0 to 4 / print(names[i]) / next i.
The **length** of an array can be found with names.length, which gives 5.
A 2D array is processed with **nested loops**: the outer loop handles rows and the inner loop handles columns.
Arrays store many items under one identifier, which is **simpler than many separate variables** and allows loops to work on all items.
Arrays are **static**: their size is fixed when declared; they cannot grow in the way a list in some languages can.
core.p: An **array** is a fixed-size data structure that stores several values of the same kind under one name, with each element accessed by its **index**. In OCR Reference Language the first index is **0**. You can declare an empty array with array names[5], which creates five elements numbered 0 to 4, or declare it with values: array colours = ["red", "green", "blue"]. An element is read or changed with square brackets, for example names[2] = "Mo". A **two-dimensional array** is like a table and needs two indexes, written grid[row,column], for example array grid[3,4] for 3 rows and 4 columns. Loops are used to process every element of an array.

bullets: Because input returns a string, you must cast with **int()** before doing arithmetic: num = int(input("Enter a number")).
Fig 5: for word = "HELLO", word.length is 5 and word.subString(1,3) is "ELL".
Concatenation with **+** joins strings: "Hi " + name; to join a number you must first convert it with str().
Data types to know: **integer** (whole number), **real/float** (decimal), **Boolean** (True/False), **character** (one symbol) and **string** (text).
ASC and CHR link to character sets: A is 65, B is 66, and a lowercase letter has a code 32 higher than its capital.
random(1,6) simulates a dice roll and can produce 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 (both ends included).
Forgetting to cast is a common cause of a **logic or runtime error**, for example comparing a string "10" with the number 5.
core.p: A **string** is a sequence of characters. OCR Reference Language provides string handling functions: word.length gives the number of characters, word.subString(start, count) returns a section starting at position start (counting from 0) and taking count characters, word.left(n) gives the first n characters and word.right(n) gives the last n. word.upper and word.lower change the case. ASC("A") gives the character code of a letter (65) and CHR(65) gives the letter back. **Casting** changes the data type of a value: int("7") gives the integer 7, float("2.5") gives the real number 2.5 and str(7) gives the text "7". A random whole number between two values inclusive is produced with random(1,6).

bullets: Example: function triple(number) / return number * 3 / endfunction, then answer = triple(4) stores **12**.
Procedure example: procedure greet(name) / print("Hello " + name) / endprocedure is called with greet("Sam").
A **parameter** is the variable name in the subprogram definition; the **argument** is the actual value passed in when it is called.
**Local variables** exist only inside the subprogram, while **global variables** can be used throughout the program; local variables are safer because they cannot be changed by mistake elsewhere.
Advantages: **code reuse**, shorter programs, easier debugging and testing, and easier teamwork.
In a flowchart a subprogram call is shown with the **subroutine symbol** (double-sided rectangle).
Link to other topics: using subprograms is part of **decomposition** and structured programming.
core.p: A **subprogram** is a named block of code that performs a specific task and can be called whenever needed. A **procedure** carries out actions but does not give a value back, whereas a **function** always **returns** a value to the place where it was called. Both can accept **parameters**, which are values passed in when the subprogram is called. In OCR Reference Language a function is written function name(parameters) ... return value ... endfunction and a procedure procedure name(parameters) ... endprocedure. Subprograms reduce repetition, make programs shorter, easier to test and easier to read, and allow several programmers to work on different parts.

bullets: Typical pattern: **open**, then **loop reading lines** until endOfFile(), then **close**.
Closing the file is important because it **releases the file** and makes sure the data is saved properly.
Writing: myFile.writeLine(name) adds a line of text to the file.
Files let a program store **high scores, settings and records** between runs.
Link to other topics: file data is stored on secondary storage (Paper 1), unlike variables in RAM.
core.p: Programs often need to store data permanently, so they read from and write to **files**. In OCR Reference Language a file is opened with myFile = open("data.txt"), a line is read with myFile.readLine(), a line is written with myFile.writeLine("text") and the file must be closed afterwards with myFile.close(). A new file is created with newFile("name.txt"). To process a whole file you loop until the end using endOfFile(), for example while NOT myFile.endOfFile(). Files keep data after the program ends, which variables cannot do because they are lost from memory.

bullets: Set up one **column per variable**, plus output, and fill in the starting values first.
Update **only the variable that changes** on each line; copy unchanged values down or leave them blank, but be consistent.
Re-test the loop condition with the **new values** every pass; the loop ends when the test fails (while) or passes (until).
Write the output in the output column in the order it is produced.
Once finished, describe in words what the algorithm achieves, e.g. 'it totals the numbers 1 to 3'.
A useful check: compare your final answer with a quick mental calculation of what the algorithm should do.
Trace tables are good evidence of **testing** for the program development stage.
core.p: A **trace table** is a table used to test an algorithm by hand. There is one column for each variable (plus a column for any condition and for output) and a new row is filled in each time a value changes. You follow the algorithm line by line, writing exactly what the computer would do, without assuming what the algorithm is meant to do. Trace tables help you find **logic errors**, check that an algorithm produces the correct output for given test data, and work out what an unknown algorithm does. Fig 4 shows the trace table for the while loop that adds 1, 2 and 3 and outputs 6.

bullets: **Syntax error**: breaks the language rules (e.g. missing endwhile); the program will not run.
**Logic error**: wrong behaviour from correct syntax (e.g. wrong operator, off-by-one in a loop).
Common exam errors to spot: wrong comparison operator, loop that never ends, wrong starting value, variable not reset, mis-spelt variable name, missing endif.
Use **test data**: normal (expected), boundary (limits such as 0 and 100) and erroneous (invalid) values.
Refinement ideas: add **validation**, use meaningful names, use subprograms, remove repeated code and add comments.
Link to other topics: **testing and debugging** and **defensive design** (input validation, authentication) all appear in the same section of the spec.
core.p: There are two main types of error. A **syntax error** breaks the rules of the language, for example a missing endif or a misspelt keyword, and stops the program from running at all. A **logic error** means the program runs but gives the wrong result, for example using < where <= was needed or starting a loop at the wrong value. Logic errors are harder to find because no error message appears, which is why we use trace tables and test data. To **refine** an algorithm you make it more efficient, clearer or more robust, for example by replacing repeated code with a loop, adding input validation or using a function. OCR also expects you to **complete** partly written algorithms and to correct algorithms with deliberate mistakes.

bullets: Use **meaningful variable names** and consistent indentation; this makes your logic easy for the examiner to follow.
Do **not** leave out output: if the question says 'display the result', include a print.
Check the **loop boundaries** (inclusive end value) and the direction of comparison signs.
If the question mentions a limit (e.g. 3 attempts), you need a **counter** that increases and a condition using it.
Validation questions need a loop that keeps asking until the input is **valid**, e.g. while score < 0 OR score > 100.
Add short **comments** where helpful but never use them in place of code.
core.h: Writing good algorithms in the exam
core.p: To score full marks on a writing question, plan before you write. First underline the **inputs, processes and outputs** in the question, then decide which structures you need: input, selection, iteration, arrays or subprograms. Write neat, indented lines in the reference language or your chosen language, declare variables before using them, and make sure each part of the question is done. Finally test the algorithm mentally with one normal and one tricky value. Marks are usually given for each required idea, such as taking input, a correct loop, a correct condition, updating a variable, and producing output, so even an incomplete answer can earn marks if the pieces are clear.

exam: **State/Identify (1 mark)**: give one short fact, e.g. 'Rounded rectangle (terminator)' for the start/end symbol.
**Describe what the algorithm does (2 to 3 marks)**: say its purpose in plain terms, e.g. 'it adds up the numbers from 1 to 3 and outputs the total', not a line-by-line list.

**Trace table questions (3 to 5 marks)**: fill every cell neatly, start with initial values, update one variable per row and include the output; marks go for correct values, not just the final answer.
**Complete the algorithm/flowchart (1 to 4 marks)**: read the surrounding lines first; the missing part must match the variable names and the loop or decision it sits in.
**Identify the error (1 to 2 marks)**: quote the line and state the problem, e.g. 'the condition should be <= not <', and say whether it is syntax or logic.
**Write an algorithm (up to 6 or more marks)**: marks are for input, the correct loop, the correct selection, updating variables and output; plan these before writing.
Use **keywords of the reference language** exactly: endif, endwhile, next, endfunction, endprocedure.
Keep **indentation** consistent so loops and ifs are clearly separate.
For 'explain why' questions, give a **reason**, e.g. 'a function is used so the code can be reused without rewriting it'.
Always check **boundary values** (e.g. exactly 18, exactly 100) when conditions use < or <=.
If stuck, write something: partial algorithms still earn marks for input, a loop or output.

mistakes.r: Use a parallelogram for input and output; the rectangle is for processes.
mistakes.w: A rectangle is used for input or output in a flowchart.

mistakes.r: A decision has two exits, labelled Yes and No (or True and False).
mistakes.w: The decision diamond has only one exit, or the exits are not labelled.

mistakes.r: Use the comparison operator ==, as in if x == 5 then.
mistakes.w: Writing x = 5 as a condition in an if statement.

mistakes.r: Both ends are included, so it runs 5 times: i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
mistakes.w: Saying for i = 1 to 5 runs 4 times.

mistakes.r: In OCR Reference Language the first element has index 0.
mistakes.w: Using index 1 for the first element of an array.

mistakes.r: input returns a string; use int() or float() before calculating.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to cast input before doing arithmetic.

mistakes.r: MOD gives the remainder, DIV gives the whole number of times it divides: 17 MOD 5 = 2 and 17 DIV 5 = 3.
Write one row per change so every variable is shown after each line or pass; marks are for the process as well as the final answer.
mistakes.w: Describing a trace table result without showing each pass.

mistakes.r: That is a syntax error; a logic error lets it run but gives the wrong answer.
mistakes.w: Describing a logic error as one that stops the program from running.

summary: You must be able to read, write, complete, trace and correct algorithms using flowcharts and OCR Reference Language pseudocode, including sequence, selection, iteration, arrays, strings, subprograms and file handling. It matters because Paper 2 questions ask you to interpret, complete and write algorithms and to trace them with trace tables.

A flowchart diamond that asks a question and has two exits, usually Yes and No.
Instructions carried out one after another in order.
A construct that chooses which instructions to run depending on a condition (if, elseif, else, switch).
Repeating a set of instructions using a loop.
A loop that repeats a set number of times, such as a for loop.
A loop that repeats while or until a condition is met, such as while or do until.
A named memory location whose value can change as the program runs.
A named value that cannot change while the program runs.
A fixed-size structure that stores several items of the same data type under one name, accessed by an index.
A named block of code that performs a task and can be called from elsewhere; a function or a procedure.
A value passed into a subprogram when it is called.
A table used to follow the values of variables line by line when testing an algorithm by hand.
A mistake that breaks the rules of the programming language so the program cannot run.
A mistake that lets the program run but produces incorrect results.

worked.q:
[4 marks] Complete a trace table for this algorithm and state the output.
x = 20
y = 0
while x > 0
  if x MOD 3 == 0 then
    y = y + x
  endif
  x = x - 4
endwhile
print(y)
steps: Start: x = 20, y = 0. Test x > 0: True.
Pass 1: 20 MOD 3 = 2, not 0, so y stays 0. x becomes 16.
Pass 2: 16 MOD 3 = 1, so y stays 0. x becomes 12.
Pass 3: 12 MOD 3 = 0, so y = 0 + 12 = 12. x becomes 8.
Pass 4: 8 MOD 3 = 2, so y stays 12. x becomes 4.
Pass 5: 4 MOD 3 = 1, so y stays 12. x becomes 0.
Test x > 0: 0 > 0 is False, so the loop ends. print(y).

while attempts < 3 AND loggedIn == false

    loggedIn = true
  else

endwhile

endif

After the loop: if loggedIn is still false, print 'Account locked'.
